questions.scenario: Imagine two bowls, each containing 100 ml of water at 20°C. One bowl is placed in a sunny spot, while the other is kept in a cool, shaded area.
questions.question: Explain which bowl's water will evaporate faster and why.
marking_criteria: Identify the effect of temperature on evaporation rate.
Explain the role of sunlight in increasing evaporation rate.
State the conclusion based on the conditions provided.
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain which bowl's water will evaporate faster and why — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Identify the effect of temperature on rate.; the role of in increasing rate.; the conclusion based on the conditions provided.
questions.model_answer: The bowl in the sunny spot will have water that evaporates faster. Higher temperatures increase the kinetic energy of water molecules, causing them to escape into the air as vapour more quickly. Sunlight also adds energy to the water, further speeding up the evaporation process.
questions.explanation: Evaporation is faster at higher temperatures because the increased energy causes more water molecules to turn into vapour.

questions.scenario: Imagine two bowls, each containing 100 ml of water at 20°C. One bowl is placed in a sunny spot, while the other is kept in a cool, shaded area.
questions.question: Describe the process of evaporation and how it leads to the cooling of the remaining water.
marking_criteria: Describe the process of evaporation.
Explain how the phase change from liquid to gas affects temperature.
Link the process to the cooling of the remaining water.
hints: Stay focused on this: Describe the process of evaporation and how it leads to the cooling of the remaining water — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: how the phase change from to gas affects.
questions.model_answer: Evaporation is the process where water changes from a liquid to a gas. As the fastest-moving water molecules escape into the air, the remaining water loses energy, causing its temperature to drop. This is because the molecules with higher energy (and thus higher temperature) are the ones that evaporate first.
questions.explanation: When water evaporates, the energy required to change from liquid to gas is taken from the remaining water, causing it to cool.

questions.scenario: A science class is observing the water cycle in a small ecosystem they have created. They place a bowl of water under direct sunlight and another in a shaded area.
questions.question: Describe what happens to the water molecules in each bowl during the process of evaporation.

Explanation of the role of energy in evaporation
hints: Stay focused on this: Describe what happens to the water molecules in each bowl during the process of evaporation — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Description of the process of evaporation; Explanation of the role of in evaporation.
questions.model_answer: During evaporation, water molecules gain energy from the sun or ambient heat and change from a liquid state to a gaseous state, becoming water vapor. In the sunny bowl, the higher temperature and energy from sunlight cause more water molecules to evaporate quickly, while in the shaded bowl, fewer molecules gain enough energy to evaporate, resulting in a slower rate.
questions.explanation: Describe the transition of water molecules from liquid to gas and the role of energy in this process.

questions.scenario: A student is investigating how wind affects the drying time of wet clothes. They hang two identical wet shirts outside on a windy day and a still day.
questions.question: Which shirt do you think will dry faster? Explain your answer.
marking_criteria: Explanation of the effect of wind on evaporation rate
Comparison of conditions on a windy day versus a still day
hints: Structure your answer around both demands: Which shirt do you think will dry faster; then Explain your answer. Make sure you also cover: Explanation of the effect of on rate; Comparison of conditions on a day versus a day.
questions.model_answer: The shirt hung on a windy day will dry faster because the wind removes the water vapor from the surface of the shirt more quickly, allowing more water to evaporate. On a still day, the water vapor remains around the shirt, slowing down the evaporation process.
questions.explanation: Explain how wind aids in the evaporation process by removing water vapour from the surface of the clothes.

questions.scenario: A student is investigating how wind affects the drying time of wet clothes. They hang two identical wet shirts outside on a windy day and a still day.

Prediction of results under different temperature conditions

questions.model_answer: On a cold day, both shirts would take longer to dry because the lower temperature reduces the energy available for water molecules to evaporate. The wind would still help to some extent by removing water vapor, but the overall rate of evaporation would be slower compared to a warmer day.
questions.explanation: Predict that lower temperatures will slow down the evaporation process and explain how temperature affects the energy available for evaporation.

questions.scenario: A science class is conducting an experiment to observe the process of boiling. They heat two identical pots of water on a stove. One pot is filled to the brim with water, while the other pot is half-filled with water.
questions.question: Explain why the water in the pot that is filled to the brim takes longer to boil than the water in the half-filled pot.
marking_criteria: Explanation of heat distribution
Explanation of surface area
Connection to boiling point
hints: Stay focused on this: Explain why the water in the pot that is filled to the brim takes longer to boil than the water in the half-filled pot — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Explanation of distribution; Explanation of; Connection to point.
questions.model_answer: The water in the pot that is filled to the brim takes longer to boil because it has more water to heat up. The heat has to distribute itself over a larger volume of water, which takes more time. Additionally, the surface area exposed to the heat is smaller in the full pot, which also slows down the boiling process.
questions.explanation: Consider the volume of water and the surface area exposed to the heat source.

questions.scenario: A science class is conducting an experiment to observe the process of boiling. They heat two identical pots of water on a stove. One pot is filled to the brim with water, while the other pot is half-filled with water.
questions.question: Describe what happens to the water molecules in each pot as the water approaches its boiling point.
marking_criteria: Description of molecular movement
Explanation of phase change
hints: Think about how the water molecules behave at different temperatures.
questions.model_answer: As the water in each pot approaches its boiling point, the water molecules gain energy and move faster. In the half-filled pot, the molecules reach the energy level required to turn into gas (steam) more quickly because there is less water to heat. In the full pot, it takes longer for the molecules to gain enough energy to boil because there is more water to heat.
questions.explanation: Consider the energy required for the phase change from liquid to gas.

questions.question: Which paper towel do you think will dry the fastest? Explain your answer.
marking_criteria: Correct identification of the fastest drying paper towel
Accurate explanation based on environmental conditions
hints: Consider the effect of temperature and humidity on evaporation.
questions.model_answer:
Paper towel A is placed in a warm, dry room. Warmth increases the rate of evaporation, and dry air has a lower concentration of water vapor, which also increases the rate of evaporation. Therefore, paper towel A will dry the fastest.

Paper towel A will dry the fastest.
questions.explanation: Explain why the paper towel placed in a warm, dry environment will dry faster than the others.

questions.scenario: A science class is observing the boiling points of different liquids. They heat samples of water, alcohol, and oil in identical containers until they boil.
questions.question: Explain why water has a higher boiling point than alcohol and oil.
marking_criteria: Explanation of the strength of intermolecular forces in water.
Comparison of intermolecular forces in water, alcohol, and oil.
hints: Consider the types of bonds present in each liquid.
questions.model_answer: Water has a higher boiling point than alcohol and oil because it has stronger hydrogen bonds between its molecules, which require more energy to break and allow the molecules to escape into the gas phase.
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds are stronger than the bonds in alcohol and oil, so more energy is needed to boil water.

questions.scenario: A science class is observing the boiling points of different liquids. They heat samples of water, alcohol, and oil in identical containers until they boil.
questions.question: Describe what happens to the molecules in each liquid as they approach their boiling point.
marking_criteria: Description of the molecular behaviour in water.
Description of the molecular behaviour in alcohol.
Description of the molecular behaviour in oil.
hints: Stay focused on this: Describe what happens to the molecules in each liquid as they approach their boiling point — develop the idea fully rather than listing short points. Make sure you also cover: Description of the molecular behaviour in; Description of the molecular behaviour in; Description of the molecular….
questions.model_answer: As they approach their boiling point, the molecules in water, alcohol, and oil gain more kinetic energy and move faster. In water, the hydrogen bonds break, allowing the molecules to escape into the gas phase. In alcohol, the weaker intermolecular forces break, allowing the molecules to escape. In oil, the even weaker intermolecular forces break, allowing the molecules to escape.
questions.explanation: As the temperature increases, the molecules gain energy and move faster, eventually breaking the intermolecular forces and escaping into the gas phase.
